extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and scholars of literature and theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing the defining features, historical variants, and examples of the dramatic/literary genre tragicomedy — i.e., works that combine tragic and comic elements. The page explains classical precedents, Renaissance theories, stylistic traits, and modern/postmodern manifestations across theatre, film, and television.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of tragic and comic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragicomedy is a literary genre that blends aspects of both tragic and comic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most often seen in dramatic literature; can describe a tragic play which contains enough comic elements to lighten the overall mood or a serious play with a happy ending. (Opening definition and overview examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended audience response: catharsis and laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragicomedy 'invokes the intended response of both the tragedy and the comedy in the audience, the former being a genre based on human suffering that invokes an accompanying catharsis and the latter being a genre intended to be humorous or amusing by inducing laughter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The genre aims to produce both emotional responses (seriousness/pain leading to catharsis) and amusement/laughter in the same work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious action with a happy ending (Renaissance/Aristotelian sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: A meaning traced to Aristotle and Renaissance writers: a serious action that concludes happily (a 'serious play with a happy ending').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical precedent: Aristotle discussed tragedy with a dual ending; Renaissance theorists and critics often understood tragicomedy as seriousness tempered by a resolution that avoids the tragic's unhappy ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedia a lieto fine (Cinthio's formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic story told with a happy or comic ending ('tragedia a lieto fine').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giovanni Battista Giraldi Cinthio argued this version of tragicomedy was better suited for staged performance; emphasizes plot outcome as the decisive factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modulated action; balance between comedy and tragedy (Guarini)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guarini's tragicomedy offered 'modulated action that never drifted too far either to comedy or tragedy,' with mannered characters and often a pastoral setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continental tragicomedy staples: moderation/ balance of tone, stylized characters, and pastoral milieus; these became conventions for the genre for a long period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of deaths; nearness to death (Fletcher's event-based criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fletcher: 'A tragi-comedie is not so called in respect of mirth and killing, but in respect it wants deaths, which is enough to make it no tragedy, yet brings some neere it, which is inough to make it no comedie.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fletcher's definition focuses on events (particularly the lack of actual deaths) and on how close the action comes to death — genre determined by presence/absence of fatal outcomes and their suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic features: revelations, outré plots, distant locales, elaborate rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragicomedy (in some English developments) had unifying stylistic features: 'sudden and unexpected revelations, outré plots, distant locales, and a persistent focus on elaborate, artificial rhetoric.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stylistic markers (not just plot outcomes) help identify works in the tragicomic mode in early modern English practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of emotions: seriousness stimulating laughter (Lessing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessing defined tragicomedy as a mixture of emotions in which 'seriousness stimulates laughter, and pain pleasure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on emotional interplay rather than plot mechanics; tragicomic effect arises from concurrent or alternating emotional tones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affinity with satire, dark comedy, absurdist and postmodern tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragicomedy is often linked with satire, 'dark' comedy or gallows humor and has affinities with absurdist drama and postmodern/metamodernist literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners cited include Pirandello, Beckett, Tom Stoppard, Dürrenmatt, and modern writers like David Foster Wallace; implies that thematic darkness plus ironic or comedic framing is characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-medium application: films and television as tragicomedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern film and television works are frequently described as tragicomedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: films (Life is Beautiful, Parasite, Jojo Rabbit, The Banshees of Inisherin, Beau Is Afraid, Mary and Max, Robot Dreams, Memoir of a Snail) and TV series (Succession, Killing Eve, Breaking Bad, Better Call Saul, Fleabag, I May Destroy You, BoJack Horseman, South Park, Moral Orel, Barry, Made for Love, The White Lotus). This indicates the genre's applicability beyond theatre into screen media.
